questions.passage: (1) In the fourteenth century, caravans moving between the Mali Empire and North African market towns did more than transport goods; they knit together two regions whose economies depended on each other. (2) Gold from the Niger River valley traveled north, while salt from Saharan mines traveled south, and neither region could supply both essentials in sufficient quantity. (3) Timbuktu, located near the river and the desert’s edge, became a meeting point where merchants exchanged not only metal and mineral but also books, rumors, and methods of accounting. (4) Historians often describe this trade as a simple exchange of gold for salt, but such a description hides the fragile arrangements that made it possible. (5) Caravan leaders depended on local guides who knew where wells would remain reliable after seasonal rains; they also relied on political agreements that allowed safe passage across lands controlled by different rulers. (6) When a drought weakened the wells or a dispute closed a route, prices in both Timbuktu and North African markets rose sharply. (7) Thus the ledger of a caravan was never merely a record of profit. (8) It was a map of trust, risk, and the practical knowledge that turned a desert into a road. (9) Modern readers may be tempted to see this trade as an early experiment in globalization. (10) Yet its scale was limited by the very conditions that sustained it: the need for local expertise, the scarcity of water, and the constant negotiation of political authority. (11) The caravan trade, in other words, prospered not because the desert disappeared but because people learned to interpret its dangers. (12) That lesson remains relevant whenever we measure the health of a long-distance market by the movement of goods alone.
questions.q: In sentence (4), the contrast between “often describe” and “hides” mainly serves to
options: question a common summary of the trade by suggesting that it leaves out crucial conditions
suggest that the trade was too mysterious for historians to study
shift the passage from historical analysis to personal recollection
praise historians for capturing the full complexity of caravan commerce
questions.explanation: “Hides” signals skepticism: the writer argues that the familiar gold-for-salt summary conceals the fragile arrangements detailed later. The other choices misread the critical tone or invent a shift not supported by the passage.

questions.topic: Rhetorical situation: audience, purpose and context
questions.passage: (1) When the Cedar River climbed over its banks last spring, the town of Bellview did not wait for a perfect plan. (2) Volunteers moved sandbags at dawn, a mosque opened its kitchen, and the high school gym became a shelter before the county had printed its first advisory. (3) Later, officials praised the “resilience” of our residents, but resilience is too tidy a word for what happened. (4) What saved us was not toughness in general but a stubborn habit of listening: to the retired engineer who noticed the water gauge rising faster than the forecast, to the grocery clerk who knew which streets flooded first, and to the grandmothers who insisted that the church van could reach the east side when the main road could not. (5) These were not experts in any formal sense, yet their knowledge had been tested by ordinary life. (6) By contrast, the outside consultants arrived with maps that showed Bellview as a single blue risk zone. (7) Their models were useful, but they could not see the ditch behind the Alvarez house or the culvert that had been clogged since August. (8) The town's recovery, then, offers a lesson for other communities facing storms: emergency plans should begin with local memory and then add technical expertise, not the other way around. (9) This is not a rejection of science. (10) It is a demand that science arrive as a partner, ready to ask questions, rather than as a rescuer certain of every answer. (11) Bellview still needs stronger levees, better drainage, and money for families whose homes are gone. (12) But it also needs to remember why the first sandbag line formed so quickly: because people trusted the neighbors who knew the ground beneath their feet.
questions.q: In the passage, the writer's primary purpose is to
options: praise volunteers for ignoring the county's early advisories.
convince officials that outside consultants should never be used again.
argue that emergency planning should combine local knowledge with technical expertise.
describe the exact sequence of events that occurred during the Bellview flood.
questions.explanation: The passage uses the flood story to advance a claim about how communities should prepare for disasters: local memory should guide and inform technical expertise. The exact sequence of events is only supporting material, and the passage explicitly rejects the idea that outside help should be abandoned.

illustrate how a librarian's approach helped the writer become engaged with reading.

questions.topic: Rhetorical situation: audience, purpose and context
questions.passage: (1) When our town's health department launched the 'Water First' campaign, some residents saw another lecture about personal choices. (2) But the campaign is not a scolding; it is an experiment in making the healthful choice the easy one. (3) In May, the city installed ten water-bottle filling stations in parks and outside the public library. (4) Each station displays a simple line: 'Cold water, no line, no sugar.' (5) At the same time, five corner stores agreed to place bottled water at eye level and move sugary drinks to the bottom shelf. (6) These changes may sound small, yet they alter the environment in which hundreds of students make a daily decision. (7) Critics argue that people should simply use willpower. (8) Willpower, however, is easier to practice when a cold refill is within a block and a soda costs two dollars. (9) In a survey of 420 high-school students conducted by the student health club, 63 percent said they would drink more water if refill stations were closer to the athletic fields. (10) The city has now added two stations near those fields. (11) A campaign that only posts warnings would likely have ended there. (12) This one listened. (13) Of course, a filling station cannot erase every barrier to health. (14) Our neighborhoods still lack affordable fresh produce, and some families have work schedules that leave little time for cooking. (15) The campaign should be one piece of a broader effort, not a trophy to display after a single summer. (16) Still, the 'Water First' effort deserves support because it treats public health as a shared design problem rather than a private test of character.
questions.q: In sentence (1), the writer's reference to 'some residents' primarily serves to
options: concede that the health department should abandon the campaign
introduce a personal conflict that the rest of the passage resolves
summarize survey data that will be analyzed in detail later
acknowledge a common skeptical reaction before the writer reframes the campaign
questions.explanation: The opening names a familiar objection—that the campaign is just another lecture about personal choices—so the writer can immediately contrast that view with the campaign's environmental approach. The passage does not analyze survey data in the first sentence, describe a personal conflict, or recommend abandoning the campaign.

Title: The Barrel Makers of Marrow Creek
(1) In 1911, when the railroad finally reached Marrow Creek, Kansas, the town's future appeared to be packed in wooden barrels.
(2) Ranchers shipped salted beef in barrels, grocers received flour in barrels, and the small cooperage beside the depot hummed from dawn until dark.
(3) For decades, the craft's rhythms shaped the town: apprentices stacked white oak staves in the yard, coopers fitted them with iron hoops, and the smell of shaved wood drifted over the school playground.
(4) Then, in the 1950s, steel drums and fiberboard boxes began replacing wooden barrels across the region.
(5) Many residents assumed the Marrow Creek cooperage would close within a year.
(6) Instead, its owner, Elena Ruiz, shifted production toward aging rooms for small wineries and distilleries, where oak still contributed flavor as well as shape.
(7) The work became more specialized: coopers selected wood by grain, toasted barrel interiors over open flames, and tested each finished barrel for leaks.
(8) By the 1980s, the cooperage employed only nine people, but its barrels traveled to restaurants in Chicago, Seattle, and New York.
(9) Today, visitors can watch a cooper split a log with a froe, a tool that looks like a long-handled knife.
(10) The craft survives not because Marrow Creek resisted change but because its workers found a new use for an old skill.
(11) The town's economy remains modest, and the cooperage is not a major employer.
(12) Yet the shop's persistence offers a lesson: traditions can be carried forward not only by preserving them exactly but also by adapting the parts that remain valuable.
questions.q: In sentence 3, the writer's use of the list of apprentices stacking staves, coopers fitting hoops, and shaved wood drifting over the school playground primarily serves to
options: criticize the cooperage for polluting a nearby school
stress that each worker performed a narrowly technical task without connection to the others
evoke the cooperative, sensory atmosphere of the town's barrel-making trade
show that the railroad had made traditional tools obsolete
questions.explanation: The list places several concrete actions and a sensory detail in parallel, creating a picture of shared, physical labor rather than isolated technical tasks. The pollution and obsolete-tool readings are unsupported by the neutral, appreciative tone.

Title: The Rams' Second Half
(1) At halftime, the Riverside Rams trailed by two touchdowns, and the locker room smelled of oranges and wet turf.
(2) Coach Amara Diallo did not raise her voice.
(3) She knelt on the concrete floor, spread a play sheet across a bench, and asked her players one question: "What have we been doing when we forget to think?"
(4) The room went quiet.
(5) On the field, the Rams had been playing as if speed alone could erase confusion; they had rushed passes, missed blocks, and left the middle of the field open.
(6) Diallo pointed to three plays on the sheet, each one simple enough for a freshman to run.
(7) "We are not going to win the second half in one throw," she said.
(8) "We are going to win it in fives: five yards, five seconds, five players doing the same small thing together."
(9) When the team returned to the field, the difference was not dramatic.
(10) The quarterback, Jonah Kim, handed the ball off again and again, accepting short gains while the clock moved.
(11) The line, led by Nia Patel at left guard, began to hold its ground.
(12) By the fourth quarter, the Rams had cut the lead to six points.
(13) They lost by one when a last-second field goal drifted wide.
(14) Yet the final score was not the lesson.
(15) The lesson was visible in the huddle before that final drive: eleven players breathing together, listening for the call, and no longer sprinting in separate directions.
questions.q: In sentences 2 and 3, the details about Coach Diallo not raising her voice and kneeling on the floor primarily serve to
options: portray her as calm and focused despite the team's difficult halftime situation
criticize the players for ignoring her instructions
suggest that she is uncertain about which plays to call
emphasize that the locker room is too crowded for a normal team talk
questions.explanation: Diallo's quiet voice, kneeling posture, and pointed question convey calm, deliberate leadership in a tense moment. The passage does not suggest uncertainty, overcrowding, or player disregard; those readings conflict with her focused authority.

questions.passage: (1) For years, our city treated traffic as a plumbing problem: if more cars surged into downtown, we widened the pipes. (2) That approach worked until it did not. (3) Every new lane invited more drivers, and soon the expanded roads were as congested as the old ones. (4) Last spring, the city council approved a different plan: convert two downtown lanes into bus-only corridors, add protected bike paths, and charge a small fee for solo drivers entering the core during rush hour. (5) Critics call the plan a war on cars, but that slogan mistakes the goal. (6) The goal is not to punish drivers; it is to give commuters real choices. (7) A nurse leaving the hospital at 7:00 p.m. should not have to choose between a forty-minute wait for a crowded bus and a fifty-minute drive through stop-and-go traffic. (8) A parent dropping a child at school should be able to ride a safe bike path instead of circling the block for a parking spot. (9) When buses move reliably, when biking feels safe, and when the true cost of driving is visible, people adjust. (10) Some will keep driving, and that is fine; the roads will work better for them too. (11) Opponents warn that the plan will hurt small businesses. (12) Yet cities from Minneapolis to Paris have found that fewer cars often mean more customers on foot. (13) A street that is pleasant to walk is a street where people stop, shop, and linger. (14) Our city is growing; we cannot build our way out of congestion with asphalt alone. (15) We can, however, build our way into a system that treats buses, bikes, and cars as parts of one network rather than competitors in a daily battle. (16) The council's plan is not a war on drivers. (17) It is a bet that a growing city can move people without asking every resident to move a car.
questions.q: The passage is most likely intended primarily for which audience?
options: Residents of a growing city who are weighing whether a new transportation plan serves the public good
City engineers who need technical details about how bus-only lanes are constructed
Small-business owners who have already decided to oppose the plan
Tourists who are unfamiliar with the city's transit system and need directions
questions.explanation: The passage explains the plan, anticipates objections, and appeals to commuters and residents rather than offering engineering specifications or directions. It mentions opponents and small businesses as a counterargument, but its broader purpose is to persuade the public that the plan serves the common good. Tourists and engineers are therefore too narrow or off-purpose.
